intuition: Use the tree's ordering to follow the two target nodes together. If both values are smaller than the current node, go left. If both are larger, go right. Their first split, or a node equal to a target, identifies the lowest node containing both targets.

If both target values are smaller than the current node, their lowest common ancestor must be somewhere in its left subtree. The symmetric argument applies when both are larger. Moving downward in either case preserves the answer while discarding a whole irrelevant part of the tree.

The first node where the comparisons disagree is the split point: one target lies on each side, so neither child contains them both. Equality also ends the search because a target node is an ancestor of itself. Return that existing node object rather than allocating a matching value.

steps: In the fixture with root 6, choose targets p=3 and q=5. Their values are both below 6.
Move to node 2. Both target values are above 2, so their shared search path continues into its right child.
The next node is 4. Target 3 is smaller and target 5 is larger, so the paths now diverge.
Node 4 contains both targets in its subtree, but neither of its child subtrees contains them both.
Return the existing node 4. The trainer converts that identity to value 4 after verifying it belongs to the original tree.

codeNotes.note: This symmetric branch follows a shared right search path. Each step gets closer to the deepest node that still contains both targets.
The remaining case is a split or equality with a target. It identifies the ancestor itself, and preserves the required original-node identity.

keyDecision: Stop when the target values lie on different sides or one equals the current node's value.

intuition: Searching the whole tree ignores its value ordering. If both targets lie on the same side of a node, their lowest shared ancestor must also be on that side.

Follow both target values together. Move left when both are smaller and right when both are larger. Stop at their first split, or when the current node is itself a target. That is the lowest shared ancestor.
concept.observation: Continue only while both targets lie strictly on the same ordered side.
approach: Compare both target values with the current node.
Move into their shared side when both agree.
Return the first split or target node.
concept.correctness: At a node where both targets lie on one side, all other positions can be excluded by search-tree ordering, and their lowest common ancestor remains in that shared subtree. At the first split, both targets descend from the current node but no child contains both. If the current node is a target, it is itself the lowest ancestor containing both. Hence the stop is exact.

complexity.explanation: Follow one root-to-node path, so work is proportional to tree height. No ancestor collection is required; extra memory is constant.

pitfalls: Continue only while both targets lie strictly on the same ordered side.
